clue.text: Classic horse-race, no point-to-point, right?

indicators.note: no here means without, so the following letters are taken out of the race word

parts.note: the hyphenated phrase taken as its letters
read as one compass point to another, south to east, S then E

explanation.surface: A punter asks whether a classic flat race is simply a horse race without any jumping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point-to-point' looks like the steeplechase; it is S and E, two compass points. Removing R, S and E (they sit together as RSE) from HORSERACE leaves the poet. 'Classic' is a classical author, not a racing Classic.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace was a Roman lyric poet, and a classic is a writer of ancient Greece or Rome.

clue.text: Sporting venue where foul play's severely punished

explanation.surface: A tennis or football ground where the referee comes down hard on fouls.
explanation.definitionFit: A tennis surface of asphalt or concrete is one sense; read as a strict tribunal, a stern court punishes crime harshly.

clue.text: Cross-check?

parts.note: voters mark their ballot papers with a cross, so checking those crosses a second time after a close election is this

explanation.surface: A query about verifying something from another angle.
explanation.definitionFit: A second count of votes in an election, each vote being a cross on a ballot.

clue.text: Macavity? He gets up to no good

definitions.text: Macavity? He gets up to no good

parts.words: Macavity? He gets up to no good
parts.note: Macavity is T. S. Eliot's criminal cat; a thief who climbs up buildings to steal is this kind of villain

explanation.surface: Macavity the mystery cat is always up to mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets up' is literal: this thief climbs walls and drainpipes. Macavity is the master-criminal cat in Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats.
explanation.definitionFit: A burglar who climbs into buildings, as nimble as a feline, is the thief named here.

clue.text: Carry out robbery — one may be framed

explanation.surface: A thief removes a painting from a gallery, the sort of picture that hangs in a frame.
explanation.definitionFit: To remove something secretly is to steal; a non-representational painting is the kind hung in a frame.

clue.text: One goes over the top in battle

explanation.surface: A soldier climbs out of the trench to charge in battle.
explanation.definitionFit: A woollen helmet pulled over the head; also the 1854 Crimean War battle with the Charge of the Light Brigade.

clue.text: Sergeant used to weigh stones

explanation.surface: An army sergeant uses scales to weigh rocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Sergeant Troy is the soldier in Hardy's Far from the Madding Crowd; the troy system of weights measures gems and precious metals.

clue.text: Fashionable US mission of French

parts.note: the Alamo is the old Spanish mission in San Antonio, Texas, famous for its siege
de is French for of

explanation.surface: A trendy American mission run by the French.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase for in the current style means up to date and stylish.

clue.text: Present to Kipling's policeman

parts.note: Kipling's poem The City of Sleep personifies dawn as Policeman Day

explanation.surface: A gift handed to a police officer from a Kipling story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift; it means the current time. Kipling's poem The City of Sleep has dawn as Policeman Day, who ends dreaming.
explanation.definitionFit: The present means this current time, the day now passing.

clue.text: Minimize significance of blame

explanation.surface: Someone plays down how important it is to blame people.
explanation.definitionFit: To slur over a matter is to gloss it; a slur is also a slight or reproach.

clue.text: Detailed account of player's performance

explanation.surface: A full report of how a musician performed.
explanation.definitionFit: A narration of facts in detail, and a concert given by one performer.

clue.text: Italian poet's tailless animal

indicators.note: tailless means the poet's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Giacomo Leopardi was a nineteenth-century Italian poet

explanation.surface: A creature belonging to an Italian poet that has no tail.
explanation.definitionFit: A big spotted cat of Africa and Asia is a wild creature.

clue.text: Wonderland contest for people on political committee

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means placed after the other piece

parts.note: a caucus is a party committee or meeting of members
a race is a people of common descent

explanation.surface: A contest in Wonderland for members of a political committee.
explanation.walkthrough: In Alice in Wonderland the Dodo organises a race where everyone runs in circles and all win.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's Alice has a Dodo-led race where everybody wins, the original of this name.

clue.text: Scratch golfer's standard once, we hear?

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word should be heard, not seen, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: bogey once meant the standard score for a hole, what par means today

explanation.surface: Something about the target score of a scratch golfer in years gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scratch' looks like a golf term; it is Old Scratch, the Devil. The golfing word was once a hole's standard score, and is said like the spelling for a hobgoblin.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Scratch is a name for the Devil, and a bogy is an evil spirit or demon.

clue.text: Official report not used by Financial Times

explanation.surface: A government report that the Financial Times chose not to use.
explanation.walkthrough: The Financial Times is famously printed on pink paper, so paper of the other colour is never used by it.
explanation.definitionFit: A government policy document is one sense; the other is the plain paper the pink Financial Times avoids.

clue.text: Revolting drunk makes one angry

parts.note: up means in revolt, as in the people are up in arms
tight is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: Being drunk and disorderly makes someone cross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' suggests disgusting; it means rising in revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: Tense, irritable and on edge, close to cross.

clue.text: Where those who enter for cup are cheered

definitions.text: Where those who enter for cup are cheered

parts.words: Where those who enter for cup are cheered
parts.note: entrants seem to be cup competitors applauded, but they are customers going in for a cup of tea and so refreshed

explanation.surface: A stadium where cup contenders get applause.
explanation.definitionFit: Cafes serving tea, where patrons come in for a cup and are refreshed.

clue.text: Sportsman allowed to enter both types of 21

parts.note: 21 is article: A is the indefinite article

indicators.note: to enter means the word for allowed goes inside the second of the two words

parts.note: and THE is the definite article
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A sportsman is permitted to take part in two kinds of event.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 across is ARTICLE, so both types are A and THE. 'To enter' puts LET inside THE.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitor in track and field events is a sporting person.

clue.text: All 12 winners.

explanation.surface: Every one of the twelve people won.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 is the Caucus Race, after which the Dodo declares that everyone has won and all must have prizes.
explanation.definitionFit: Every person, all of them; and in Carroll's Caucus Race the Dodo rules that all the runners have won.

clue.text: Piece played to hundreds at a meeting

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so two of them are CC

explanation.surface: A piece of music performed to large audiences at a gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: A keyboard composition for showing off touch and dexterity, such as Bach's for organ.

clue.text: "Moorish" grave site in Spain

parts.note: Moorish suggests the Moors of Spain, but means of Sir John Moore, buried on the Galician coast after the 1809 battle

explanation.surface: A tomb from the Moorish period somewhere in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir John Moore, killed in 1809, is the subject of the poem The Burial of Sir John Moore after this battle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Galician port, now A Coruna, where the British general was buried in 1809.

clue.text: Letters from 10 published in paper

indicators.note: published means the letters are put out afresh in a new order

parts.note: 10 across is RECITAL, whose letters are used

explanation.surface: Correspondence from Downing Street printed in a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' looks like Number 10 Downing Street; it is 10 across, RECITAL. 'Published' rearranges its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of writing that appears in a newspaper or journal.

clue.text: Artist includes bearings in peer's heraldic device

indicators.note: includes means the painter's name wraps round the directions

parts.note: Corot was a French landscape painter
N and E, north and east, are compass bearings

explanation.surface: A painter puts heraldic bearings into a nobleman's coat of arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bearings' suggests heraldry, matching the surface; it means compass directions.
explanation.definitionFit: A small crown worn or displayed by nobles below royal rank.

clue.text: Be critical of a catch

explanation.surface: Someone finds fault with a fish that was caught.
explanation.definitionFit: To complain or find fault pettily; also a freshwater fish an angler might land.

clue.text: This French author's written up material for a tanner

indicators.note: in a down clue, written up means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: sumac leaves are used in tanning leather

explanation.surface: A French writer composed a piece on leather-tanning supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert, the French novelist of The Outsider, is a writer.

clue.text: Political group of guests?

parts.note: read as a party in the House of Commons, but means a gathering of visitors staying at a country house

explanation.surface: A political faction formed by visitors.
explanation.definitionFit: A gathering of guests staying several days at a country home.

clue.text: Sailor makes disarming attempts, initially

explanation.surface: A seaman makes efforts at disarming someone.
explanation.walkthrough: SALT stands for Strategic Arms Limitation Talks, the US-Soviet negotiations of the 1970s; old salt is a seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: An experienced seaman is an old salt; the acronym names the US-Soviet arms-limitation talks.

clue.text: An excellent sleeper, in highest position

parts.note: a spinning top running so smoothly it seems still is said to sleep

explanation.surface: Someone who sleeps well is at the very peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sleeper' suggests a person or a railway beam; a spinning top that runs smoothly is said to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Placed on top of, at the summit.

clue.text: Record time

explanation.surface: A note of a record-breaking time.
explanation.definitionFit: The written record of a meeting, and sixty-second units of time.

clue.text: Main engagement for the French — seasonal show

parts.note: le is French for the
a panto, pantomime, is the British Christmas stage show

explanation.surface: A Christmas pantomime booking for a French company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' is the sea: this is the 1571 naval battle. A panto is a British Christmas family theatre show.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1571 battle in which the Holy League defeated the Ottoman fleet was fought at sea.

clue.text: Plays harp — is his section allegro?

indicators.note: section means a run of letters cut from the words shown

explanation.surface: A harpist plays a passage marked allegro.
explanation.definitionFit: Allegro means briskly, and sharpish is British slang for quickly.

clue.text: Moderately like the girls of Dublin

explanation.surface: The Dublin girls are fairly good-looking.
explanation.walkthrough: The song Molly Malone begins in Dublin's fair city, where the girls are so pretty.
explanation.definitionFit: Fairly or somewhat; and attractive, as the song about Molly Malone describes Dublin's girls.
